name: Phyllanthus niruri (stonebreaker, chanca piedra)
short: Rats: leaf extract in pregnancy caused maternal kidney changes and fetal macrosomia (large fetuses). 12-month trials in chronic hepatitis B and fatty liver disease: no serious or major adverse events.
text: In pregnant rats given an aqueous leaf extract of Phyllanthus niruri by gavage, the extract did not alter reproductive outcomes or cause birth defects, but the highest dose (600 mg/kg) changed maternal kidney weight and structure, and the extract caused fetal macrosomia (large fetuses) and increased ossification sites; the authors concluded the leaf extract can produce detrimental effects during pregnancy. A second rat study of exposure during pregnancy and breastfeeding found changes in maternal liver-function markers, and earlier opening of the ear canal and eyes and anxiolytic-like behaviour in male offspring, although its authors judged these insufficient to indicate maternal or postnatal toxicity; that abstract states that use of the plant is contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding. In people, a 12-month placebo-controlled trial in 50 people with chronic hepatitis B found no changes in kidney function and no serious adverse events due to treatment, and a 12-month randomised placebo-controlled trial of a standardised extract in 226 adults with fatty liver disease reported no major adverse events in either group. A Cochrane review of Phyllanthus species (not only P. niruri) in chronic hepatitis B, covering 16 randomised trials with 1326 patients, found that only two trials reported adverse event numbers, without significant differences, and that no serious adverse events were reported. A 2025 systematic review of human and rat studies in kidney stones said that the evidence consistently supports long-term safety, based on serial measurements of blood electrolytes and liver function, and that growing evidence suggests the herb, used alongside standard treatments, is safe without significant adverse effects, and in a retrospective study a combination of boldine with P. niruri and Ononis spinosa taken with tamsulosin had drug-related adverse effects comparable to tamsulosin alone. For interactions, a review raised only a theoretical possibility that P. niruri could increase the bioavailability of the tuberculosis medicine rifampicin through effects on drug-transporter proteins, noted that other mechanisms may reduce or eliminate this effect, and said in vivo studies are needed to confirm any interaction.
